problems.title: Complement Pair Ledger
problems.prompt: Given an integer array and a target, return the two distinct indices whose values add to the target. Exactly one valid pair exists, and an index may not be reused. Preserve every stated ordering, indexing, and tie rule.
constraints: Use the exact input and output contract above; do not silently change index, interval, or tie semantics.
Choose representations that meet the stated time and space bounds.

examples.explanation: Store 4→0 and 7→1. At index 2 the complement 9 is absent, so store 1→2. At index 3 the complement 1 maps to index 2; return [2, 3]. This trace names the maintained state so you can reproduce the transition on a new input.

learningObjectives: Translate Complement Pair Ledger into a precise state and invariant.
Contrast the direct baseline with the hash maps and sets solution.
Implement, prove, and test the O(n) / O(n) approach.

analogy.body: Think of a hash table as a labelled wall of lockers: instead of walking the whole room to find a fact, compute its locker label and inspect that location directly.
analogy.limit: Real hash tables can collide and resize, so access is expected O(1), not a universal worst-case guarantee.

hints: First write what must remain true after each hash maps and sets transition.
Use the worked trace to identify which earlier state is reused instead of recomputed.
Before coding, explain why the cases Negative values and a negative target and Duplicate values such as [3, 3] with target 6 do not violate the invariant.
problems.naiveApproach: Trying every pair is easy to verify but performs n(n−1)/2 comparisons, which becomes quadratic as the array grows. Use this version as a small-input oracle when testing the optimized implementation.
problems.approach: Scan left to right. Before inserting the current value, look up target − value in a hash map from value to an earlier index.
problems.proof: Invariant: Before processing index i, the map contains exactly the values at indices [0, i), so a successful lookup always names a distinct earlier index. Initialization satisfies this statement before any candidate is processed. The algorithm's update preserves it while permanently resolving or advancing at least one candidate. When processing ends, the invariant covers the entire input, so the reported result satisfies the contract.

examples.output: The result required by the clarified contract
examples.explanation: Trace the advanced number theory state rather than treating the algorithm as a memorized recipe.

learningObjectives: Recognize when advanced number theory applies and when it does not.
Derive the maintained state and correctness invariant before coding.
Defend time, space, edge cases, and an alternative approach in an interview.

analogy.body: Advanced number theory is like keeping a compact field notebook: record only the facts future decisions require, update them when the input changes, and avoid replaying the entire history.
analogy.limit: The notebook metaphor explains state reuse, but the exact invariant and legal transitions still depend on the problem contract.

hints: Write the advanced number theory invariant in one sentence.
Test the smallest input and an adversarial boundary before optimizing.
problems.naiveApproach: Start with the direct exhaustive method for Number-Theoretic Transform: enumerate every feasible candidate and validate it independently. This baseline is useful for testing, but it repeats state and usually misses the intended interview bound.
problems.approach: Apply Advanced number theory. Decompose modular and prime structure so expensive arithmetic becomes reusable precomputation. Define the state precisely, update only what changed, and state why discarded candidates cannot later become optimal.
problems.proof: Establish the state invariant before the first update, show that one legal transition preserves it, and show that each transition makes progress. At termination, connect the invariant to the requested result and account for every feasible candidate.
walkthrough: Write the smallest nontrivial input and initialize the exact maintained state.
Perform one transition and name every state value that changes.
Reach termination and verify the returned object against the original contract.

complexity.time: Derive from the number of state transitions
complexity.rationale: Count how often each element, vertex, edge, or state can enter and leave the maintained structure; do not quote a pattern complexity without this accounting.

misconceptions.claim: Recognizing Advanced number theory is enough to justify the solution.
misconceptions.correction: Pattern recognition suggests a candidate; the invariant and contract prove that it fits this problem.

misconceptions.claim: Passing the sample proves correctness.
misconceptions.correction: The sample illustrates one path; a proof plus adversarial boundary cases covers the input space.

misconceptions.claim: The named data structure determines the complexity automatically.
misconceptions.correction: Complexity follows from operation count, and one element may be processed more than once.

followUps: How would the design change for streaming input or online updates?
Which assumption makes the chosen bound possible, and what breaks if it is removed?
edgeCases: Empty, singleton, and minimum legal input
Duplicates, ties, disconnected state, or numeric boundaries
